Some folks are shocked we're doing Windows (client) before Linux (client) for Rex. Note we will publicly ship with full Linux and FreeBSD server support soon, but clients will come later. Why? Let's talk about it!

If you don't want to watch a [short] video, here is some commentary but I'm not including everything I said in the vidoe:

First, there are a LOT of Windows devs. Like, a LOT A LOT. In fact, based on various recent sources, there are more developers on Windows than every other desktop OS combined. And that shouldn't surprise people, but it sometimes does.

Second, Linux is hard because there are a LOT of opinions because there are LOT of ways to do things and people tend to hold their own opinions in very high regard.

I've been shipping Linux software for my whole career, and desktop Linux software almost full time the past few years, so I'm very familiar with the nuances here and we want to get it right or at least communicate it right.

Third, we found a super awesome motivated Windows (amongst other things) developer early on, so we have someone very talented already looking at it full time. We're still working through the Linux side.

It's magic being able to easily connect to a Windows Rex server from macOS (or vice versa), and more importantly for the `rex` CLI to be able to see it for automations, testing, etc. The Rex Server for Windows expanded from alpha (limited) to beta (full Discord) testing today. Getting the Rex Server to work on Windows was complicated. There is an incredible amount of Windows-specific logic throughout the Rex server everywhere...

Networking (supporting Windows named pipes and their ACLs) to terminals (windows-specific memory management) to job control (so we can detect the proper running program) to the myriad shells and ways you can run Windows programs (PowerShell, Cmd, Cygwin, plus as a user, admin, etc.).

Some super fun edge cases found during testing, for example we had to build-in detection for Entra accounts (school, work, etc.) which don't support certain features (yeah, I didn't know about Entra before either). And others...

We also have Windows-native packaging: the Rex server is available via WinGet, as an MSI, or as a plain old Zip. We support installation as a on-demand started user process, an on-login user process (no admin required), and a system service (admin required).

We're serious about Windows.

item.description:
All intelligent systems I've ever seen have exactly two adaptation timescales.

The first one is on-the-fly situation modeling. In humans, this is known as fluid intelligence. In modern AI, this is implemented via reasoning chain generation or program generation.

The second one is offline mining of a long buffer of past experiences to extract the reusable abstractions that enable on-the-fly situation modeling. In humans, this is known as long-term plasticity or connectome learning. In modern AI, this is pre-training and post-training.

Up until late 2024, AI only had the second phase -- no fluid intelligence, only storage and retrieval of patterns seen at training time.

item.title: 【回复】@sh_reya：研究发现小型大语言模型在成对比较任务中存在明显的顺序偏置与不稳定性
item.description:
回复 @sh_reya
New lab blog post! How do you run complex semantic top-k queries on your unstructured text, accurately and at scale? E.g., "which sales calls most clearly show a customer committing to buy?"

Common convention is to (1) use pairwise LLM comparisons for accuracy (e.g., "does call A show more commitment to buy than call B?"), since cosine similarity on off-the-shelf embeddings misses nuanced criteria, and (2) use small LLMs, so it's cheap at scale.

Surprisingly, we find that just asking the small LLM to score each record and sorting (a "pointwise" approach) is just as accurate (if not more) on a few business-oriented top-k tasks, and up to 13x faster in our experiments.
原帖

回复 @sh_reya
Why does pairwise do worse? Interestingly, if you swap the order of the two records in the prompt, many small LLMs pick a different record! Qwen3-0.6B basically never picks the same one; bigger models are more consistent, but even the best one we tried (Jev) still flips on a whopping 12% of pairs in one dataset!

Basically just a private Slack workspace for your agents AND developers (which can even sync to Slack channels for better observability)

The idea (not necessarily Vercel's implementation of it) makes so many things simple:

1. Collaborative grilling

Each locally running agent has its own identity on the board. As does every human!

That means if you're grilling with an agent, and you need to ask someone a question, you just get your agent to ping them (or, ping their agent!)

2. Locally running agents

This setup feels awesome for connecting locally running agents to the rest of the organisation.

"Unread messages" could form a queue (Vercel board doesn't do this AFAIK) which would allow remote agents to ping messages to local agents, which would get picked up when they wake up.

This would allow seamless communication between remote and local, and aid companies looking to make the leap to remote agents.

3. Schedules

Want to schedule a cron? Just trigger a repeating message to an agent. I love how simple it makes the mental model.

item.title: @Thom_Wolf：研究人员在飞机飞行途中测试并优化Inkling 2 Mini模型本地性能
item.description:
Really like the idea of the plane bench.

What’s the best you can get a model to ship on a MacBook with no WiFi on your typical SF<>LA plane trip

@mhrezaeics：Behind the scenes of plane bench:

Yesterday, @luke_drago_ and I asked @miramurati over lunch if we could catch “the next flight” to record Inkling 2 Mini on a plane to demonstrate its local performance without wifi. She said yes, and plane bench was born.

We were in the airport two hours later with tickets for LA. Unfortunately that flight got delayed until it was dark outside, so we couldn’t get the right lighting to record. We ended up in LA last night with two constraints:
- Our return flight was set to land just before 9am.
- Our model was set to go out around noon.

If we couldn’t get it during the ~30 minutes we were at cruising altitude and turn it around in time for the launch three hours after landing, we wouldn’t be able to land plane bench.

Because we had one chance to get this right in time for launch, we used the night in LA to optimize. We held a late night call with @ChowdhuryNeil, @simonguozirui, and @andyarditi to figure out the fastest demo we could pull off. We also pushed some optimizations including kernel improvements to make it run faster.

The video we used in the blog post was the first take from our flight this morning.
